lessons.title: Color without light
body: MeshStandardMaterial reacts to lights using a physically based shading model. MeshBasicMaterial shows its color without scene lighting. Unlit materials are useful for markers, UI-like objects, and intentionally flat graphics.

Switch the cube to a basic material and notice that its faces lose light-based shading. Geometry and position have not changed; the surface model has. A dark standard material may simply need a light.
lessons.task: Replace MeshStandardMaterial with MeshBasicMaterial for the cube.
lessons.hint: The simplified material below contains only color, which both materials accept.

quiz.question: Which material works without scene lights?
quiz.explanation: MeshBasicMaterial is unlit, so lights do not affect its color.

lessons.title: Polished or matte?
body: Roughness describes how uneven a surface is at a microscopic scale. Low values give sharper highlights; high values spread them into broader, softer reflections.
The property ranges from 0 to 1. It does not change the mesh’s actual shape. Compare this sphere at 0.08 and 0.9, watching the highlight from our directional light.
lessons.task: Set material.roughness to 0.9 for a matte finish.
lessons.hint: Change the final assignment, which overrides the constructor value.

quiz.question: Higher roughness produces…
quiz.explanation: Roughness spreads reflected light over more directions.

lessons.title: Make it metallic
body: Metals and nonmetals respond differently to light. In the standard material, metalness blends between those models. Pure materials are usually near 0 or 1; intermediate values can represent mixed or weathered surfaces.

Metals reflect their surroundings and have little diffuse response. A metal can look dark when there is little to reflect. We use strong studio lights here; production metallic scenes often also use an environment map.
lessons.hint: Keep roughness at 0.25 so the light produces a clear highlight.

quiz.question: Why might a metal look dark?
options: It has nothing bright to reflect
quiz.explanation: Metals depend strongly on reflected lighting and environments.

lessons.title: See through a surface
body: Opacity is a value from 0 (invisible) to 1 (opaque). To blend a material with what is behind it, also enable transparent. Opacity alone is not enough for the usual transparent-material workflow.

Overlapping transparent surfaces can have sorting artifacts. For this simple shell, depthWrite is disabled so it does not hide later transparent draws. That is a useful technique, not a universal cure for every transparency problem.
lessons.task: Set material.transparent to true to reveal the inner sphere.
lessons.hint: Opacity is already 0.3. Enable the separate transparent flag.

quiz.question: Which pair enables ordinary transparent blending?
quiz.explanation: transparent enables blending and opacity controls how opaque the surface is.

lessons.title: The back of a polygon
body: Triangles have a front and a back, determined by vertex order. Materials normally draw only front faces. This saves work but means a one-sided plane disappears when viewed from behind.
DoubleSide draws both sides. Try orbiting behind this plane before and after changing the material. Use it where you need a two-sided surface, rather than enabling it on every closed solid.
lessons.task: Change material.side from FrontSide to DoubleSide.
lessons.hint: Set material.side = THREE.DoubleSide, then keep needsUpdate.

quiz.question: Why can a plane disappear from behind?
quiz.explanation: With FrontSide, only the triangle’s front-facing side is drawn.
